Text 2
Varga's novel does close with that recording. But just before it, the linguist plays her tapes for village children, who mimic the phrases, garble them, and reuse them in their games. Varga presents the language not as dead but as changing hands.

The novel closes as the linguist records the dialect's last fluent speaker.
The children's games show the dialect surviving in an altered form.
The filling notebooks mirror the gradual emptying of the coastal village.

A.why: This is Text 1's conclusion, and Text 2 rejects it outright: Varga presents the language 'not as dead but as changing hands.' You picked a claim that only one author holds.

D.why: This is the subtype's trap. It's a reasonable reading of the novel's imagery, and Text 1 mentions it, but Text 2 never takes it up. You read the novel yourself instead of finding the point the two critics share.

Literary historians have generally treated *Loom Songs* (1847), a collection by mill weaver Hannah Pell, as a record of factory hardship. Its poems dwell on clattering power looms, lint-choked air, and fourteen-hour shifts; scholars therefore value it chiefly as documentary evidence of early textile labor.

Text 2
Pell's poems do catalogue the miseries of the mill floor. Yet reading them only as documents overlooks their craft: many stanzas follow the back-and-forth rhythm of a shuttle, so that the verse itself imitates weaving. Pell was a deliberate artist, not merely a witness.
choices: Loom Songs is valuable chiefly as evidence about early textile labor.
Pell patterned the rhythm of many stanzas on a shuttle's motion.
Pell wrote her poems mainly to win shorter shifts for mill weavers.
Pell's poems depict the harsh conditions of work in textile mills.

A.why: This is Text 1's position, and Text 2 is written to challenge it: reading the poems 'only as documents overlooks their craft.' Author 2 would not agree.

B.why: This is Text 2's new observation. Text 1 treats the poems purely as documentary evidence and says nothing about their rhythm, so you can't credit it to Author 1.

C.why: This is the subtype's trap. Given the poems' subject, it's a plausible guess about Pell, but neither critic says she wrote to campaign for reform. You reasoned from the poems' content instead of from what the critics argue.

Text 2

B.why: This is Text 1's conclusion, and it's exactly what Text 2 narrows: 'Ellison ridicules the fad, not the science.' Author 2 would reject it.

C.why: This is the subtype's trap. It's your own reading of a detail from the novel. Text 1 uses the bakery trips only as evidence of satire, and Text 2 ignores them, so neither critic makes this claim.

A.why: This is Text 1's reading. Text 2 rejects it directly: 'The poem concerns not loss but energy returning to use.'
